claims.text: A method combining first-principles calculations, on-the-fly machine learning, and semiclassical Boltzmann transport theory can predict lattice thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed method can achieve prediction accuracy of ±10%.
The proposed method will outperform earlier approaches.
The proposed method captures atomic-scale complexity in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed method distinguishes lattice heat transport from electronic heat transport.
The intended material may contain defects or impurities, including approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Defects and impurities are components of the atomic-scale complexity treated as the structural mediator.
The transport treatment captures phonon-phonon interactions.
The transport treatment captures electron-phonon interactions.
The predicted lattice thermal conductivity at 300 K is 5–15 W/(K m).
The predicted lattice thermal conductivity at 1200 K is 10–20 W/(K m).
The predicted lattice thermal conductivity increases between 300 K and 1200 K.
Experiments report total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m).
The prediction is intended to apply from 200 K to 1200 K.
The prediction is intended to apply to HfNbTaTiZr samples that may contain impurities such as 1 wt.% oxygen.
Prediction accuracy may depend on the machine-learning method, first-principles calculation quality, and representation of defects and impurities.
A deviation greater than 20% between measured and predicted lattice thermal conductivity would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis claims ±10% accuracy, but falsification requires an error greater than 20%, leaving errors between 10% and 20% inconsistent with the accuracy claim but non-falsifying.

The hypothesis emphasizes separating lattice and electronic transport, but the experimental design does not specify an electronic-contribution measurement or subtraction procedure needed for an unambiguous lattice-only comparison.
